question: SAP Labs Scholar@SAP technical round 2. Reported: **reverse a string using two pointers**, **types of normalization**, the **difference between HTTP and HTTPS**, **REST APIs**, Firebase, the difference between **static and dynamic memory**, and **how the garbage collector works** (plus OOP and HR questions).
lookingFor: Breadth across fundamentals with correct basics
answer:
**Reverse a string (two pointers).**
```
i = 0; j = n - 1
while i < j: swap(s[i], s[j]); i++; j--
```
O(n) time, O(1) extra space; for immutable strings (Java, Python) convert to an array first.

**Normalization types.** 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependency on a composite key), 3NF (no transitive dependency), BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Purpose: remove redundancy and update, insert and delete anomalies.

**HTTP vs HTTPS.** HTTP sends data in plain text, so anyone on the path can read or alter it. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, adding **encryption** (confidentiality), **integrity** (tamper detection) and **authentication** of the server through a certificate signed by a trusted CA. The TLS handshake agrees on keys, then data is encrypted symmetrically. Default port 443 instead of 80.

**REST API.** An architectural style over HTTP: resources identified by URLs (`/users/42`), operations through methods (GET read, POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove), stateless requests, standard status codes, and usually JSON. Statelessness makes services easy to scale horizontally.

**Static vs dynamic memory.** Static (compile-time) allocation fixes size before running: globals, static variables, and stack frames for locals. It is fast, automatic, and limited in size. Dynamic allocation happens at run time on the heap (`new`, `malloc`), with flexible size and lifetime, but it needs management (manual free in C/C++, GC in Java) and can fragment or leak.

**Garbage collector.** Automatic reclamation of heap objects that are no longer reachable. A mark-and-sweep style collector starts from roots (stack variables, statics), marks everything reachable, then sweeps the rest; compaction reduces fragmentation. Generational collectors (as in the JVM) put new objects in a young generation, collected often and cheaply, and promote survivors to an older generation, based on the observation that most objects die young. Reference counting is another approach, but it cannot free cycles on its own. GC pauses are the cost.
